title: Effects of acoustic environment on design work performance based on multitask visual cognitive performance in office space

findings.antecedent: Sound source type (music vs. traffic noise vs. natural sound vs. ambient environment vs. air-conditioning noise vs. speech)
findings.consequent: Reaction time in visual cognitive tasks
findings.statement: Different sound source types have significantly different effects on reaction time. The shortest reaction time was under music (mean = 2.560 s, SD = 1.546), followed by traffic noise, air-conditioning noise, and ambient sound. Speech yielded the longest reaction time.
findings.quote: The reaction time was the shortest in the silent environment of music (mean = 2.560 s, SD = 1.546), followed by traffic noise (mean = 2.705 s, SD = 1.716) and air-conditioning noise (mean = 2.771 s, SD = 1.844). Interestingly, the reaction time in the environment with natural sound (mean = 2.873 s, SD = 1.884) was significantly longer than in a noisy environment.

scope_conditions.setting: Laboratory office space at Harbin Institute of Technology
scope_conditions.task_context: Multitask visual cognitive work (visual search, graphical memory, location memory)
scope_conditions.participant_type: College students majoring in architecture/interior design

stimulus_description.music: Downloaded from music material library [16], calm music without obvious emotional value
stimulus_description.traffic_noise: Main street noise at 50 km/h speed
stimulus_description.natural_sound: Flowing stream sound recorded in a park in Harbin
stimulus_description.air_conditioning_noise: 0.5 m^3 1:7.5 m 0.333 s, mechanical noise level 26-40 dB
stimulus_description.speech: Introduction to the code for civil building sound insulation GB 50118-2010

findings.mechanism: Arousal level and noise distraction; natural sounds may enhance working efficiency by optimal arousal
theory_links: Arousal theory (optimal performance at medium arousal levels)
Ventral cortical pathway for visual processing
moderators_reported: Gender (men showed significantly longer reaction times than women under air-conditioning noise at 60 dB: mean difference = 0.425 s)
Noise sensitivity (high-sensitivity respondents had significantly longer reaction times than low-sensitivity respondents)
Personality traits (introversion/extroversion not significant for reaction time, p > 0.05)

source_quality_indicators.control: RTs varied between 0.3-1.5 s as step length in controlled experiment

findings.antecedent: Sound source type (music vs. traffic noise vs. air-conditioning noise vs. natural sound vs. ambient environment vs. speech)
findings.consequent: Accuracy rate in visual search tasks
findings.statement: Different sound source types have variable effects on visual search accuracy. Music and ambient environments showed highest accuracy rates (mean > 99%), while traffic noise showed lower accuracy (mean = 98.99%).
instruments_used: accuracy measurement (search accuracy, graphics accuracy, location accuracy)
findings.quote: The accuracy rate of the respondents' visual cognitive work performance (with error bars of 95% CI) in environments with different types of sound sources are shown in Fig. 4.

scope_conditions.task_type: Three subtasks: visual search, graphical memory, location memory

stimulus_description.sound_types: Music, traffic noise, air-conditioning noise, natural sound, ambient environment, speech

findings.mechanism: Attention allocation and distraction; different sounds affect concentration differently
moderators_reported: Gender effects on accuracy for graphics in different acoustic conditions
Noise sensitivity not significantly related to accuracy rates

findings.antecedent: Sound source type = music
findings.consequent: Reaction time compared to other sound source types
findings.statement: Music resulted in the shortest reaction times compared to all other sound source types, with mean = 2.560 s.
findings.quote: The reaction time was the shortest in the silent environment of music (mean = 2.560 s, SD = 1.546)

stimulus_description.music: Calm music without obvious emotional value

findings.mechanism: Optimal arousal level through musical stimulation

source_quality_indicators.comparison_basis: all conditions tested in same subjects

findings.antecedent: Sound pressure level (SPL) of traffic noise (range 45-65 dB)
findings.consequent: Reaction time
findings.statement: As traffic noise SPL increased from 45 dB to 65 dB, reaction time increased. The SPL had significant negative correlation with reaction time (r = -0.077**). At SPL > 50 dB, reaction time decreased with increasing SPL, showing a nonlinear relationship.
findings.source: Section 3.2, p. 7; Table 4, p. 7; Figure 5, p. 6
findings.quote: The reaction time decreased most significantly when the SPLs of the two noise environments changed from 60 dB to 65 dB. The reaction time was reduced by 0.234 s and 0.215 s for traffic noise and air-conditioning noise, respectively.

stimulus_description.noise_source: Traffic noise from main street vehicles at 50 km/h speed

findings.mechanism: Increased arousal from noise, attention capture, cognitive overload at higher levels

source_quality_indicators.measurement_control: Automated SPL adjustment via Adobe Audition

findings.antecedent: Sound pressure level (SPL) of air-conditioning noise (range 45-65 dB)
findings.consequent: Reaction time
findings.statement: Air-conditioning noise SPL shows significant negative correlation with reaction time (r = -0.063**). When SPL increases from 50 dB to 65 dB, reaction time decreases, especially between 60-65 dB (reduction of 0.215 s).
findings.quote: The mean values of the accuracy rate of the respondents' visual cognitive work performance (with error bars of 95% CI) with traffic and air-conditioning noise under different SPLs (45 dB, 50 dB, 55 dB, 60 dB, 65 dB) are shown in Fig. 6.
findings.mechanism: Arousal modulation and attention focusing at moderate noise levels

findings.antecedent: Traffic noise SPL (50 dB vs. 65 dB)
findings.consequent: Memory accuracy of location
findings.statement: When traffic noise increases from 50 dB to 65 dB, the memory accuracy of the location is reduced by 4.42%. At SPL of 50 dB, memory accuracy was higher; at 65 dB, memory accuracy dropped to 96.73%.
findings.quote: When the traffic noise increases from 50 dB to 65 dB, the memory accuracy of the location is reduced by 4.42%.
findings.mechanism: Cognitive load from noise distraction reduces working memory capacity

findings.antecedent: Reverberation time (RT) of speech sound (range 0.3-1.5 s)
findings.consequent: Reaction time
findings.statement: As reverberation time of speech increases from 0.3 s to 1.5 s, reaction time decreases. The reaction time is reduced by 0.274 s. However, there is a slight change in reaction time at RT increase from 0.9 s to 1.5 s.
findings.quote: The increase in the reverberation of speech will effectively shorten the reaction time and increase the memory accuracy of graphics. As the RT of speech increases from 0.3 to 1.5 s, the reaction time is reduced by 0.274 s.

stimulus_description.sound_source: Introduction to the code for civil building sound insulation GB 50118-2010

findings.mechanism: Speech clarity and intelligibility improvement with moderate reverberation

source_quality_indicators.control: RT systematically varied in 0.3 s increments

findings.antecedent: Reverberation time (RT) of speech (0.3-1.5 s) or music (0.3-1.5 s)
findings.consequent: Memory accuracy of graphics
findings.statement: The effects of RT on memory accuracy of graphics differ between speech and music. For speech, memory accuracy gradually increases by 2.49% as RT increases from 0.3 to 1.2 s. For music, effects are less pronounced.
findings.quote: The accuracy rate of the memory of the graphics shows a gradual upward trend. The accuracy rate of the memory of the graphics increases by 2.49% as the RT of speech increases from 0.3 to 1.2 s.
findings.mechanism: Sound clarity and comprehension effects on cognitive processing
moderators_reported: Sound type (speech vs. music) affects magnitude of RT effects

findings.antecedent: Reverberation time of speech
findings.consequent: Reaction time and memory accuracy of location
findings.statement: Correlation analysis showed that RTs of speech have a significant negative correlation with reaction times (r = -0.053*) and memory accuracy of location memory (r = -0.011). The effects on location memory were not significant.
findings.quote: The Spearman correlation analysis method was employed to analyze the correlation between the RTs and the reaction times with speech and music sound environments.
findings.mechanism: Sound properties affecting cognitive processing

findings.antecedent: Reverberation time of music
findings.consequent: Reaction time and work performance
findings.statement: RTs of music showed no significant correlation with reaction times (r = -0.018) or memory accuracy rates, with no significant effects on visual cognitive work performance.
findings.quote: The RTs of the music do not correlate with the accuracy rates in speech and music sound environments.
findings.mechanism: Music processing differs from speech processing

findings.antecedent: Gender (male vs. female participants)
findings.consequent: Reaction time under air-conditioning noise at 60 dB
findings.statement: Men showed significantly longer reaction times than women under air-conditioning noise at 60 dB (mean difference = 0.425 s).
findings.quote: The results are shown in Fig. 9. Significant differences emerged mainly in SPLs from 55 dB to 60 dB, with a few at 65 dB and the natural sound acoustic environment (p < 0.01 or p < 0.05). The most significant gap in reaction time between men and women was 0.425 s, which occurred in the music environment.
findings.mechanism: Gender-based differences in noise sensitivity or task strategy
moderators_reported: Specific SPL levels (55-65 dB) and sound types

findings.antecedent: Gender (male vs. female)
findings.consequent: Memory accuracy of graphics in air-conditioning and natural sound environments
findings.statement: In air-conditioning and natural sound environments, memory accuracy of graphics for men was significantly lower than for women (p < 0.01).
findings.quote: sound environments significantly impacted the memory accuracy of graphics and the memory accuracy of location. For instance, in the 0.3 s RT music sound environment, the memory accuracy of location of men was significantly lower than that of women (p < 0.01).
findings.mechanism: Gender-based differences in visual-spatial memory or attentional processes under acoustic stress
moderators_reported: Acoustic environment type

findings.antecedent: Gender (male vs. female)
findings.consequent: Memory accuracy of location under different acoustic conditions
findings.statement: In the 0.3 s reverberation time (RT) music sound environment, men's memory accuracy of location was significantly lower than women's (p < 0.01).
findings.quote: For instance, in the 0.3 s RT music sound environment, the memory accuracy of location of men was significantly lower than that of women (p < 0.01).
findings.mechanism: Gender differences in spatial memory under acoustic conditions
moderators_reported: Specific RT level (0.3 s) and sound type (music)

findings.antecedent: Noise sensitivity (high vs. low)
findings.consequent: Reaction times under different acoustic conditions
findings.statement: Reaction times of high-sensitivity respondents were significantly longer than those of low-sensitivity respondents in different sound environments (p < 0.01 or p < 0.05), indicating that high noise-sensitive individuals respond more slowly to visual tasks in noisy conditions.
findings.source: Section 4, Discussion, p. 9; Figure 9, p. 9; Table 3, p. 4
findings.quote: In terms of noise sensitivity, the results showed that the reaction times of high-sensitivity respondents were significantly longer than those of low-sensitivity respondents in different sound environments.

stimulus_description.assessment_tool: 21-item Noise Sensitivity Scale using 6-point Likert scale

findings.mechanism: Individual differences in auditory sensitivity and distraction susceptibility
moderators_reported: Multiple acoustic conditions show significant differences

findings.antecedent: Personality trait (introversion vs. extroversion)
findings.consequent: Visual cognitive work performance (reaction time and accuracy)
findings.statement: Personality traits (introversion/extroversion) showed no significant impact on visual cognitive work performance (p > 0.05). The accuracy rates in different acoustic environments were not influenced by personality characteristics.
findings.quote: Therefore, it was concluded that personality traits have no significant impact on visual cognitive work performance.

stimulus_description.assessment: Personality Extraversion Test E-Scale (21 items, Yes/No format)

findings.mechanism: No identified mechanism; personality type does not moderate task performance

findings.antecedent: Musical preference (enjoy music or not)
findings.consequent: Reaction times in music environment
findings.statement: Reaction times of respondents who listen to music regularly were significantly shorter than those who rarely listen to music in the music sound environment (p < 0.01 or p < 0.05).
findings.source: Section 4, Discussion, p. 9; Figure 9, p. 9; Table 3, p. 4
findings.quote: times of respondents used listening to music were significantly shorter than those of respondents who were not, in a different sound environment condition (p < 0.01 or p < 0.05).

stimulus_description.assessment: Self-report questionnaire on music listening frequency

findings.mechanism: Familiarity and comfort with musical stimuli reduces distraction
moderators_reported: Effect specific to music environment

findings.antecedent: Sound pressure level (SPL) and sound source type interaction
findings.consequent: Combined effects on visual cognitive work performance
findings.statement: The combined effects of sound source type and SPL on visual cognitive performance show that traffic and music noise could effectively reduce reaction time, while air-conditioning noise shows more complex effects across SPL levels.
findings.quote: Relative to other sound environments, the ambient sound environment (mean = 2.838 s, SD = 1.535), music and traffic noise could effectively reduce the reaction time of visual cognitive

scope_conditions.interaction_factors: Sound source type and SPL level

stimulus_description.sound_types: Traffic noise, air-conditioning noise, music, speech, natural sound, ambient environment at SPLs 45-65 dB

findings.mechanism: Different noise types have differential arousal and distraction effects at varying intensity levels
moderators_reported: SPL level
Sound source type

findings.antecedent: Acoustic environment quality in office spaces
findings.consequent: Worker visual cognitive performance and design work productivity
findings.statement: Improving the acoustic environment in office spaces is significant for promoting workers' visual cognitive work performance. Acoustic design should be considered as an important factor in office space design.
findings.quote: In this paper, a multitask visual cognition experiment was conducted. The differences in visual cognitive work performance of 41 respondents under different acoustic conditions were compared. This proves that improving the acoustic environment office space is significant to promote employees' visual cognitive work performance.
findings.mechanism: Optimal acoustic conditions reduce cognitive load and support sustained attention

findings.antecedent: Speech sound reverberation time (0.3-1.5 s)
findings.consequent: Intelligibility and reaction time
findings.statement: Increased reverberation time of speech will effectively shorten reaction times (reducing by 0.274 s from 0.3 to 1.5 s) and increase memory accuracy of graphics (by 2.49% from 0.3 to 1.2 s), suggesting optimal acoustic conditions support cognition.
findings.quote: The increase in the reverberation of speech will effectively shorten the reaction time and increase the memory accuracy of graphics. As the RT of speech increases from 0.3 to 1.5 s, the reaction time is reduced by 0.274 s.

stimulus_description.speech_content: Introduction to code for civil building sound insulation GB 50118-2010

findings.mechanism: Improved speech clarity at moderate reverberation times reduces cognitive effort
moderators_reported: Effects specific to speech (not music)

findings.antecedent: SPL of traffic noise > 50 dB
findings.consequent: Reaction time decrease rate
findings.statement: When traffic noise SPL exceeds 50 dB, reaction time decreases with increasing SPL. Most significantly, between 60-65 dB SPL, reaction time decreases by 0.234 s.
findings.quote: The reaction time decreased most significantly when the SPLs of the two noise environments changed from 60 dB to 65 dB. The reaction time was reduced by 0.234 s and 0.215 s for traffic noise and air-conditioning noise, respectively.
findings.mechanism: Arousal modulation; increased noise may enhance alertness up to a point

findings.antecedent: SPL of air-conditioning noise (60-65 dB)
findings.consequent: Reaction time
findings.statement: When air-conditioning noise SPL increases from 60 to 65 dB, reaction time decreases by 0.215 s, showing a significant reduction in high-SPL conditions.
findings.quote: The reaction time was reduced by 0.234 s and 0.215 s for traffic noise and air-conditioning noise, respectively.
findings.mechanism: Arousal enhancement at high noise levels

findings.antecedent: Memory accuracy rate relationships with SPL (traffic and air-conditioning noise)
findings.consequent: Spearman correlation between SPL and search accuracy, graphics accuracy, location accuracy
findings.statement: SPL of traffic noise has significant negative correlation (r = -0.077**) and air-conditioning noise (r = -0.063**) with reaction time, but shows minimal or non-significant correlation with memory accuracy measures.
findings.quote: The Spearman correlation analysis method was used to analyse the correlation among SPL, RT, reaction time, and accuracy rate.

stimulus_description.noise_types: Traffic noise and air-conditioning noise at 45-65 dB

findings.mechanism: SPL effects on speed of processing are stronger than on accuracy

findings.antecedent: Design acoustic environment with sound source type optimization
findings.consequent: Work performance in office design tasks
findings.statement: In designing the interior acoustics of office spaces, music can be used to cover other noises. Natural sounds should be avoided using the main design strategy to design indoor soundscapes.
findings.quote: In designing the interior acoustics of the office space, music can be used to cover other noises. In addition, the speech intelligibility of speech in an office should be considered by architects based on reasonably controlling the noise levels.

stimulus_description.design_consideration: Sound source selection for office spaces

findings.mechanism: Music provides beneficial arousal; natural sounds may not support task performance

findings.antecedent: Optimal SPL for office design (traffic noise SPL of 50 dB; air-conditioning noise SPL of 55 dB)
findings.consequent: Visual cognitive work performance
findings.statement: Based on experimental results, the recommended maximum SPL for traffic noise is 50 dB, and for air-conditioning noise is 55 dB for office spaces to maintain optimal visual cognitive work performance.
findings.quote: Therefore, the experimental results of this research can provide references for the sound insulation design of building facades. For instance, when the traffic noise increases from 50 dB to 65 dB, the memory accuracy of the location is reduced by 4.42%. The accuracy rate is the main evaluation criterion for visual cognitive work performance. It is recommended to design an open-plan layout.

stimulus_description.recommended_levels: Traffic noise 50 dB, air-conditioning noise 55 dB

findings.mechanism: These levels balance arousal benefits against cognitive overload

source_quality_indicators.basis: Performance degradation measured at higher SPLs

findings.antecedent: High reverberation time (RT > 1.0 s) in speech environments
findings.consequent: Speech intelligibility and cognitive task performance
findings.statement: High reverberation times of speech (1.2-1.5 s) show a plateau effect where further increases do not substantially improve reaction time or memory accuracy beyond 1.2 s RT, suggesting diminishing returns.
findings.quote: However, there is a slight change in reaction time at RT increase from 0.9 s to 1.5 s. However, in the case of human speech, the respondents' reaction time gradually decreases and the memory accuracy of graphics gradually increases as the RT increases.
findings.mechanism: Optimal reverberation around 0.9-1.2 s; further increases do not enhance performance

findings.antecedent: Complex multitask visual cognitive work (three subtasks: visual search, graphical memory, location memory)
findings.consequent: Overall performance depends on three aspects
findings.statement: Visual cognitive work performance in office design depends on three balanced aspects: visual search ability, memory accuracy of graphics, and memory accuracy of location. Different acoustic conditions differentially affect these three aspects.
instruments_used: E-Prime multitask visual cognition experiment system
findings.source: Section 2.2, Methodology, p. 3; Section 3, Results, p. 5
findings.quote: In the current study, visual cognitive work performance depended on three aspects: visual search ability, memory of graphics, and memory of the location.

stimulus_description.tasks: Finding target graphics, identifying shapes, recalling locations

findings.mechanism: Office work requires integrated visual, spatial, and memory capabilities
moderators_reported: Each aspect shows different acoustic sensitivity

findings.antecedent: Noise environment exceeding 50 dB SPL (traffic noise) or 55 dB SPL (air-conditioning)
findings.consequent: Memory accuracy of location
findings.statement: Noise levels above optimal thresholds (50 dB for traffic, 55 dB for air-conditioning) result in progressive reduction of location memory accuracy. The maximum suggested SPL for traffic noise is 50 dB, and for air-conditioning noise is 55 dB.
findings.quote: Therefore, the maximum suggested SPL for traffic noise is 50 dB, and that of air-conditioning noise is 55 dB.
findings.mechanism: Cognitive overload and distraction increase with noise beyond thresholds

findings.antecedent: Individual characteristics (gender, noise sensitivity, personality, music preference)
findings.consequent: Visual cognitive task performance variability
findings.statement: Different individual characteristics moderate performance under acoustic conditions. Significant moderators include gender, noise sensitivity, and music preference, while personality traits (introversion/extroversion) do not significantly affect performance.

sample.demographics: 18 women, 23 men; high noise sensitivity n=25, low n=26; introverts n=16, extroverts n=25; regular music listeners n=29, infrequent n=12

findings.quote: Apart from the impact of the acoustic environment, the individual characteristics of workers in office space also affect the work performance in office space. Individual characteristics include gender, noise sensitivity, and personality traits (introversion/extroversion).

stimulus_description.characteristics_examined: Gender, noise sensitivity, personality, music preference

findings.mechanism: Individual differences in auditory processing, attention, and stimulus evaluation
moderators_reported: Gender (significant)
Noise sensitivity (significant)
Music preference (significant)
Personality (not significant)

findings.antecedent: Research on acoustic environment and single cognitive work vs. multitask visual cognitive work
findings.consequent: Knowledge gap regarding multitask performance
findings.statement: Previous studies focused mainly on single cognitive work; research on acoustic environment effects on multitask visual cognitive work is lacking, which the current study addresses through a comprehensive multitask experiment.
findings.quote: Most previous studies are dedicated to investigating single cognitive work. Research focusing on designing multitask visual cognitive work is lacking.

stimulus_description.gap: Lack of multitask cognitive performance studies

findings.mechanism: Real office work involves multiple simultaneous cognitive demands

findings.antecedent: Study population characteristics (college students majoring in architecture/interior design)
findings.consequent: Ecological validity for office design work context
findings.statement: The study used college students from architecture/interior design (n=41, ages 22-27 years, mean 24.43) as representatives of design professionals. This population performs similar visual cognitive tasks (finding graphics, identifying properties, recalling locations) to professional designers.

sample.education: College students majoring in architecture/interior design

findings.source: Section 2.4, Selection of Respondents, p. 4; Table 3, p. 4
findings.quote: 41 college students majoring in architecture or interior design from Harbin Institute of Technology, and engaged in visual cognition work, were selected as the respondents, comprising 18 women (average age = 24.43 years, SD = 2.47) and 23 men (average age = 24.01 years, SD = 2.56).
findings.mechanism: Design students' visual task skills are relevant to professional designer work

source_quality_indicators.field_relevance: Design majors perform similar visual tasks

findings.antecedent: Sound environment parameters systematically varied (sound source type, SPL, RT)
findings.consequent: Comprehensive characterization of acoustic effects
findings.statement: The study systematically manipulated three major acoustic parameters: sound source type (6 types), sound pressure level (45-65 dB in 5 dB steps), and reverberation time (0.3-1.5 s in 0.3 s steps) to comprehensively characterize acoustic environment effects.
findings.quote: In this study, five representative sound sources (speech, traffic noise, natural sound, music) were selected as the sound samples. Ambient environment was chosen as the reference for acoustic comparison.

scope_conditions.systematic_variation: 6 sound types × 5 SPL levels × 5 RT levels

stimulus_description.sound_types: Speech, traffic noise, air-conditioning, music, natural sound, ambient

findings.mechanism: Comprehensive parametric design allows identification of acoustic effects across dimensions
moderators_reported: All three acoustic dimensions systematically varied

findings.antecedent: Balanced performance model incorporating memory accuracy (graphics and location), reaction time, and acoustic parameters
findings.consequent: Predictive equation for visual cognitive work performance
findings.statement: A balanced performance model was developed incorporating three outcome measures (reaction time, memory accuracy of graphics, memory accuracy of location) with acoustic parameters. The model is: PI = (Ag)^x (At)^y S^z, where PI is performance index, Ag is graphics memory accuracy, At is location memory accuracy, and S is reaction time reciprocal.
findings.quote: A balanced performance model is given in the following form: PI = (Ag)^x (At)^y S^z, where PI refers to the performance index, Ag refers to the memory accuracy of the graphics, At refers to the memory accuracy of the location, and S refers to the reciprocal of the reaction times.
findings.mechanism: Integrated performance model balances speed and accuracy tradeoffs
moderators_reported: Model parameters can be calibrated for specific design scenarios

source_quality_indicators.basis: Empirical data from 41 participants across all conditions

limitations: Sample size of 41 college students limits generalization to professional designers and other age groups
Young adult population (mean age 24.43 years) may not represent older workers' acoustic sensitivity
Laboratory setting with artificial acoustic environment may not fully represent real office spaces
Study population limited to architecture/interior design students; results may not generalize to other office worker types
Individual characteristics measured via self-report (music listening, personality traits)
Reverberation time manipulation via Adobe Audition may not perfectly replicate natural room acoustics
Cross-sectional design; no longitudinal assessment of acoustic adaptation effects
Speech material limited to single language (Chinese) and single content domain
Gender distribution relatively unbalanced (18 women, 23 men)
No assessment of stress, cognitive workload, or subjective fatigue during tasks

Cognitive load theory: mechanism for acoustic environment effects on working memory

Psychoacoustics: individual differences in noise sensitivity and acoustic perception
Environmental psychology: role of workplace acoustic design in worker performance
Speech intelligibility theory: effects of reverberation time on comprehension and task performance
Speed-accuracy tradeoff: integration of reaction time and accuracy in performance metrics
Occupational ergonomics: application to office design and worker productivity
